method: Samples per frame is the audio sample rate divided by the frame rate, and the page keeps that division exact rather than rounding it. 48 kHz at 25 fps is 1,920 samples per frame with nothing left over, while 48 kHz at 29.97 fps is 1,601.6, so no whole number of samples fits every frame boundary. The fractional rates are the 1001-denominator time bases, not rounded decimals: 23.976 fps is 24000/1001, 29.97 is 30000/1001, 47.952 is 48000/1001 and 59.94 is 60000/1001, which is why 48 kHz at 23.976 fps is exactly 2,002 samples per frame and 44.1 kHz at 29.97 fps is 147,147 samples per 100 frames. The page reduces the ratio to its lowest terms and reports the exact fraction, the whole samples a frame can hold (the floor and the ceiling), how many frames take each, the frames and samples in the repeating cycle, and the start of that cycle. A frame boundary sits at floor(frame x samples per frame) and a frame carries the difference between its own boundary and the next, so every boundary is within one sample of the exact position and the rounding never accumulates: at 29.97 fps the five-frame cycle runs 1,601, 1,602, 1,601, 1,602 and 1,602. The page also prices the flat whole count that editors, cameras and DAWs usually use, because truncating costs sync: a fixed 1,601 samples per frame at 48 kHz loses three samples every five-frame cycle, which is 600 samples or 12.5 ms after 1,000 frames. Frame numbers are plain integers counted from 0 where frame 0 starts at sample 0, not timecodes, and the result is arithmetic for aligning double-system sound, building an audio-only timeline or checking a sync offset, not a converter: it does not resample, retime, shift pitch, apply a 0.1% audio pull-up or pull-down, read drop-frame timecode or model any device's own clock, buffer or converter latency. Frame rates are limited to the ten listed time bases, sample rates to 44.1, 48, 88.2 and 96 kHz, and frame numbers to 10,000,000, about 46 hours at 60 fps, with the sample position kept exact over that whole range. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.
